```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(nlmixr2lib)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Choquette_2017_lidocaine_dog"))$reference`
* Description: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Choquette_2017_lidocaine_dog"))$description`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169745> (open access)
* Supplement: S1 Table, the individual plasma lidocaine concentrations
  (<https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169745.s001>)

Choquette et al. compared three compartmental models fitted jointly to the
plain and the adrenalinated formulation. The selected Model C (Fig 1C of the
paper) has one disposition compartment with apparent clearance CL/F and volume
V/F shared by both formulations, and two parallel zero-order inputs per
formulation:

* a fraction `f` of the dose enters the plasma at a constant rate
  `k01 = f * Dose / Dur1` from the dose time until `Dur1`;
* the remaining `1 - f` enters at `k02 = (1 - f) * Dose / Dur2` from the delay
  `tau` until `tau + Dur2`.

`f`, `Dur1`, `Dur2` and `tau` were estimated separately for each formulation.
In the packaged model the binary covariate `CONMED_EPI` (1 = adrenalinated)
selects the parameter set. Each administration is two dose records carrying the
same amount, one into `depot` (the early absorption compartment `Xa1`) and one
into `depot2` (the late compartment `Xa2`); `f()` splits the dose and `alag()`
applies `tau`.

# Population

Eight healthy female beagles aged 2 to 5 years and weighing 11 (SD 1.3) kg
received a paravertebral brachial plexus block under isoflurane anaesthesia
(Methods, Animals and Study design). Lidocaine hydrochloride 20 mg/mL, alone or
with adrenaline 0.01 mg/mL, was diluted 1:1 with saline and injected at 2 mg/kg
on each of three nerve roots (C6, C7 and C8-T1), 6 mg/kg in total, within four
minutes. A randomised, blinded crossover over three periods gave 10 plain and 9
adrenalinated profiles, each sampled 13 times to 180 minutes (Results). The
population was fitted by maximum-likelihood expectation maximisation in ADAPT 5
with log-normal parameters and a diagonal covariance matrix.

```{r population}
str(readModelDb("Choquette_2017_lidocaine_dog")()$population)
```

# Source trace

Table 1 of the paper reports each model parameter as the arithmetic mean (SD) of
a log-normal distribution. The model stores the median,
`mean / sqrt(1 + CV^2)`, and the log-scale variance `log(1 + CV^2)`, with
`CV = SD / mean`.

| Equation / parameter | Value (Table 1, mean (SD)) | Source location |
|----------------------|----------------------------|-----------------|
| One-compartment disposition with two parallel zero-order inputs | n/a | Fig 1C; Methods, Pharmacokinetic analysis |
| `lcl` (CL/F, both formulations) | 0.017 (0.005) L/min/kg | Table 1 |
| `lvc` (V/F, both formulations) | 1.850 (0.580) L/kg | Table 1 |
| `lfdepot_plain`, `lfdepot_adr` (f) | 0.56 (0.22); 0.54 (0.15) | Table 1 |
| `ld1_plain`, `ld1_adr` (Dur1) | 5.77 (3.24); 11.30 (7.05) min | Table 1 |
| `ld2_plain`, `ld2_adr` (Dur2) | 18.10 (4.87); 254.00 (129.00) min | Table 1 |
| `ltlag_plain`, `ltlag_adr` (tau) | 6.52 (0.02); 3.87 (0.03) min | Table 1 |
| `eta*` variances | `log(1 + (SD/mean)^2)` of each row above | Table 1; Methods (diagonal covariance) |
| `k01`, `k02` | derived, `f * Dose / Dur` | Fig 1C |
| `propSd` | fixed at 0 | not reported |
| Per-kg scaling of CL/F and V/F by `WT` | n/a | Table 1 units (L/min/kg, L/kg) |

# Structural checks

A typical-value solve of each input path on its own must reproduce the
closed-form constant-rate infusion into one compartment, and the two paths
must add up to the combined solve. A dense grid and tight tolerances make the
comparison a test of the model code rather than of the integrator.

```{r structure, message = FALSE}
mod <- readModelDb("Choquette_2017_lidocaine_dog")
mod_typ <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod)
th <- mod_typ$theta

wt <- 11
dose <- 6 * wt # mg lidocaine hydrochloride (6 mg/kg)
cl <- exp(th[["lcl"]]) * wt
vc <- exp(th[["lvc"]]) * wt
kel <- cl / vc

grid <- c(0, seq(0.05, 600, by = 0.05))

path_events <- function(epi, cmts) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(time = 0, evid = 1, amt = dose, cmt = cmts),
    data.frame(time = grid, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(id = 1L, WT = wt, CONMED_EPI = epi)
}

infusion <- function(t, rate, t0, dur) {
  ifelse(
    t <= t0, 0,
    ifelse(
      t <= t0 + dur,
      rate / kel * (1 - exp(-kel * (t - t0))),
      rate / kel * (1 - exp(-kel * dur)) * exp(-kel * (t - t0 - dur))
    )
  ) / vc
}

checks <- lapply(c(plain = 0, adrenalinated = 1), function(epi) {
  sfx <- if (epi == 0) "plain" else "adr"
  f <- exp(th[[paste0("lfdepot_", sfx)]])
  d1 <- exp(th[[paste0("ld1_", sfx)]])
  d2 <- exp(th[[paste0("ld2_", sfx)]])
  tau <- exp(th[[paste0("ltlag_", sfx)]])
  solve <- function(cmts) {
    as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ, path_events(epi, cmts),
      rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12, maxsteps = 1e6
    ))
  }
  early <- solve("depot")
  late <- solve("depot2")
  both <- solve(c("depot", "depot2"))
  ref_early <- infusion(early$time, f * dose / d1, 0, d1)
  ref_late <- infusion(late$time, (1 - f) * dose / d2, tau, d2)
  data.frame(
    formulation = if (epi == 0) "plain" else "adrenalinated",
    max_abs_err_early = max(abs(early$Cc - ref_early)),
    max_abs_err_late = max(abs(late$Cc - ref_late)),
    max_abs_err_sum = max(abs(both$Cc - (early$Cc + late$Cc))),
    tmax_early = early$time[which.max(early$Cc)],
    Dur1 = d1,
    peak = max(both$Cc)
  )
})
checks <- dplyr::bind_rows(checks)
knitr::kable(checks, digits = 6)

stopifnot(
  # Each path is the closed-form infusion (the table shows < 1e-6 mg/L).
  all(checks$max_abs_err_early < 1e-5),
  all(checks$max_abs_err_late < 1e-5),
  # Superposition: the two paths add up to the combined dose.
  all(checks$max_abs_err_sum < 1e-5),
  # A constant-rate input with no other input peaks at the end of the input.
  all(abs(checks$tmax_early - checks$Dur1) <= 0.05)
)
```

The total exposure of a combined dose obeys `CL * AUC(0-inf) = Dose` (CL/F and
V/F are apparent values, so the absorbed fraction is folded into them). Both
formulations share CL/F, so they must give the same AUC(0-inf) even though the
adrenalinated input lasts more than four hours.

```{r mass-balance, message = FALSE}
long_grid <- c(0, seq(0.5, 3000, by = 0.5))
auc_inf <- sapply(c(0, 1), function(epi) {
  ev <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(time = 0, evid = 1, amt = dose, cmt = c("depot", "depot2")),
    data.frame(time = long_grid, evid = 0, amt = 0, cmt = "central")
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(id = 1L, WT = wt, CONMED_EPI = epi)
  s <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(mod_typ, ev, rtol = 1e-10, atol = 1e-12))
  sum(diff(s$time) * (head(s$Cc, -1) + tail(s$Cc, -1)) / 2)
})
auc_inf
stopifnot(all(abs(cl * auc_inf / dose - 1) < 1e-3))
```

# Virtual cohort

Two arms of 200 virtual beagles, one per formulation, with body weight drawn
from the reported 11 (SD 1.3) kg and kept inside 8 to 14 kg by redrawing. Each
dog receives 6 mg/kg lidocaine hydrochloride as one administration at time 0
(the paper treats the three injections given within four minutes as a single
dose). Observations are on the `central` state.

```{r cohort}
set.seed(20170109)
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20170109)

draw_wt <- function(n) {
  w <- rnorm(n, 11, 1.3)
  while (any(bad <- w < 8 | w > 14)) w[bad] <- rnorm(sum(bad), 11, 1.3)
  w
}

obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(0, 30, by = 0.5), seq(31, 180, by = 1))))

make_arm <- function(n, epi, id_offset) {
  subj <- data.frame(
    id = id_offset + seq_len(n),
    WT = draw_wt(n),
    CONMED_EPI = epi
  )
  doses <- subj |>
    tidyr::crossing(cmt = c("depot", "depot2")) |>
    dplyr::mutate(time = 0, evid = 1L, amt = 6 * WT)
  obs <- subj |>
    tidyr::crossing(time = obs_times) |>
    dplyr::mutate(cmt = "central", evid = 0L, amt = 0)
  dplyr::bind_rows(doses, obs) |>
    dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      formulation = if (epi == 0) "Plain" else "Adrenalinated"
    )
}

events <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  make_arm(200, 0, 0L),
  make_arm(200, 1, 200L)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(events[, c("id", "time", "evid", "cmt")]))
```

# Simulation

```{r simulate}
sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = c("formulation", "WT")) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

# Replicate published figures

Figure 2 of the paper shows the individual profiles. The observed summaries
below were computed by the maintainers from the paper's S1 Table: the 19
profiles were pooled by formulation, grouped into sampling-time windows, and
summarised as the median and interquartile range of the concentrations in each
window.


```{r figure-2, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
# Replicates Figure 2 of Choquette 2017: plasma lidocaine after 6 mg/kg
# paravertebral lidocaine, plain (A) and adrenalinated (B).
vpc <- sim |>
  dplyr::group_by(formulation, time) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Q05 = quantile(Cc, 0.05),
    Q50 = quantile(Cc, 0.50),
    Q95 = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(vpc, aes(time, Q50)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q05, ymax = Q95), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(
    data = observed,
    aes(time, cmed, ymin = c25, ymax = c75),
    colour = "firebrick", size = 0.3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(formulation, c("Plain", "Adrenalinated"))) +
  labs(
    x = "Time after the first injection (min)",
    y = "Plasma lidocaine (mg/L)",
    title = "Simulated median and 90% interval vs observed median and IQR",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 2 of Choquette 2017 (observed data from S1 Table)."
  )
```

The simulated median follows the observed median through the absorption,
peak and elimination phases for both formulations, including the plateau of
the adrenalinated profile, in which the late input (median duration about four
hours) runs slower than elimination.

```{r figure-2-check}
sim_at_obs <- observed |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sim_med = {
      ff <- formulation
      tt <- time
      v <- vpc[vpc$formulation == ff, ]
      stats::approx(v$time, v$Q50, xout = min(tt, 180))$y
    }
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(log_ratio = log(sim_med / cmed))

sim_at_obs |>
  dplyr::filter(time > 10) |>
  dplyr::group_by(formulation) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    `median log(sim/obs)` = median(log_ratio),
    `90th pct abs log(sim/obs)` = unname(quantile(abs(log_ratio), 0.9)),
    `max abs log(sim/obs)` = max(abs(log_ratio)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)

# Windows before 10 min mix samples taken 2 min after each of the three
# injections and are left out. After that the simulated median is centred on
# the observed medians; the largest misses are in the adrenalinated windows
# between 10 and 20 min, where the observed median itself goes 1.16, 1.03,
# 1.73 mg/L from one window to the next (7 to 16 samples each). The gate is on
# the centre and on the 90th percentile of the misses: a mis-transcribed CL/F,
# V/F, f or duration shifts a whole phase and breaks both.
stopifnot(
  with(subset(sim_at_obs, time > 10), abs(median(log_ratio)) < 0.15),
  with(subset(sim_at_obs, time > 10), quantile(abs(log_ratio), 0.9) < 0.4)
)
```

# PKNCA validation

```{r pknca}
conc <- sim |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, formulation)
conc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  conc,
  conc |> dplyr::distinct(id, formulation) |> dplyr::mutate(time = 0, Cc = 0)
) |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, formulation, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time)

dose_df <- events |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1, cmt == "depot") |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, formulation)
stopifnot(nrow(dose_df) == 400L)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, Cc ~ time | formulation + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | formulation + id)
intervals <- data.frame(
  start = 0, end = 180,
  cmax = TRUE, tmax = TRUE, auclast = TRUE
)
nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))
```

# Comparison against published NCA

Table 1 of the paper reports Cmax, tmax and AUC(0-tlast) from the observed data
(last sample at 180 min) as log-normal means. The simulated values are
the medians of 200 virtual dogs per formulation.

```{r nca-compare}
published <- data.frame(
  formulation = c("Plain", "Adrenalinated"),
  cmax = c(2.944, 1.847),
  tmax = c(19.72, 13.53),
  auclast = c(281.8, 215.9)
)

cmp <- nlmixr2lib::ncaComparisonTable(
  simulated = nca,
  reference = published,
  by = "formulation",
  units = c(cmax = "mg/L", tmax = "min", auclast = "min*mg/L"),
  tolerance_pct = 20
)
knitr::kable(cmp)
if (!is.null(attr(cmp, "footnote"))) cat(attr(cmp, "footnote"))

sim_med <- as.data.frame(nca$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD %in% c("cmax", "auclast")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(formulation, PPTESTCD) |>
  dplyr::summarise(med = median(PPORRES), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = med) |>
  dplyr::left_join(published, by = "formulation", suffix = c("_sim", "_pub"))

# Cmax and AUC are the exposure metrics; a wrong CL/F, V/F, f or duration
# moves them by tens of percent. tmax is not gated: the adrenalinated
# profiles are nearly flat after the early input, so tmax is ill-defined.
stopifnot(
  all(abs(sim_med$cmax_sim / sim_med$cmax_pub - 1) < 0.15),
  all(abs(sim_med$auclast_sim / sim_med$auclast_pub - 1) < 0.15)
)
```

The disposition parameters give a terminal half-life of
`r signif(log(2) / (0.017 / 1.850), 3)` min from the Table 1 means of CL/F and
V/F, matching the paper's 75.0 min. Adrenaline lowers the simulated median
Cmax by about
`r round(100 * (1 - sim_med$cmax_sim[sim_med$formulation == "Adrenalinated"] / sim_med$cmax_sim[sim_med$formulation == "Plain"]))`%
(paper Table 1: 37%) and AUC(0-180) by about
`r round(100 * (1 - sim_med$auclast_sim[sim_med$formulation == "Adrenalinated"] / sim_med$auclast_sim[sim_med$formulation == "Plain"]))`%
(paper: 23%).

The plain-formulation tmax is flagged: the simulated median is about 24 min
against the 19.7 min of Table 1. The observed tmax in the S1 Table, computed by
the maintainers from the individual profiles, has a median of 23.6 min and a
mean of 23.4 min for the plain formulation, close to the simulation; the
plain profiles have a broad peak between about 17 and 31 min (Figure 2), so a
small change in the samples moves tmax by several minutes.

# Reported zero-order rates

Table 1 also lists `k01` and `k02` in mg/min. In Model C the zero-order rates
are fixed by the other three parameters, `k0 = f * Dose / Dur`, so the packaged
model derives them rather than carrying them as separate parameters. Their
tabulated values are not on the same scale as the doses used in the study: the
Table 1 means imply rates near `f / Dur` per unit dose, and products such as
`k01 * Dur1` (0.43 plain, 0.42 adrenalinated) fall short of the reported `f`
(0.56, 0.54). The table below shows the rates implied by the Table 1 means of
`f` and `Dur` for a 6 mg/kg dose.

```{r k0}
k0 <- data.frame(
  formulation = c("Plain", "Adrenalinated"),
  f = c(0.56, 0.54), Dur1 = c(5.77, 11.30), Dur2 = c(18.10, 254.00),
  k01_table = c(0.075, 0.037), k02_table = c(0.013, 0.001)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `k01 implied (mg/min/kg)` = f * 6 / Dur1,
    `k02 implied (mg/min/kg)` = (1 - f) * 6 / Dur2,
    `k01 * Dur1 (Table 1)` = k01_table * Dur1,
    `k02 * Dur2 (Table 1)` = k02_table * Dur2
  )
knitr::kable(k0, digits = 3)
```

The ratios between formulations agree with the paper either way (k01 halved and
k02 about 90% lower with adrenaline), and the typical-value solve built from
`f` and `Dur` reproduces the observed Cmax and AUC, which a rate on the scale
of the tabulated `k01` and `k02` would not.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Parameter scale.** Table 1 gives each parameter as "log-normal mean
  (log-normal SD)". These were read as the arithmetic mean and SD of a
  log-normal distribution and converted to the median and the log-scale
  variance (see Source trace). Reading the means as medians instead would raise
  every typical value by between under 0.001% (tau) and 18% (Dur1, adrenalinated).
* **Parameterisation of the inputs.** Model C lists `f`, `Dur1`, `Dur2`, `tau`,
  `k01` and `k02` for each formulation, but a zero-order input that empties its
  compartment ties `k0 = f * Dose / Dur`. The model carries `f`, `Dur1`, `Dur2`
  and `tau` (the quantities in Fig 1C's dose split and arrows) with their
  Table 1 variability; the Table 1 SDs of `k01` and `k02` are not used. See
  "Reported zero-order rates" for why the tabulated `k0` values cannot be used
  as rates directly.
* **`tau` is measured from the dose time.** The paper calls `tau` the delay to
  the onset of the late absorption phase and draws it on the late compartment
  only (Fig 1B/1C). The adrenalinated `tau` (3.87 min) is shorter than its
  `Dur1` (11.30 min), so the two inputs overlap; the model allows this.
* **Cap on `f`.** `f` is log-normal, so about 4% of plain and 1% of
  adrenalinated draws exceed 1. The model caps `f` at 1 so that the late
  fraction `1 - f` is never negative.
* **Residual error.** The ADAPT 5 variance model is not reported. `propSd` is
  fixed at 0, so simulations carry between-dog variability only.
* **Repeated dosing.** The zero-order rates use the amount and time of the
  most recent dose into each absorption compartment, which is exact for a
  single administration and for administrations whose inputs do not overlap.
  The study gave one administration (three injections within four minutes,
  treated by the authors as a single dose).
* **Abstract wording.** The abstract and Results state that adrenaline
  decreased Cmax and `tau` "by approximately 60%". Table 1 gives ratios of
  0.63 (Cmax) and 0.59 (`tau`), that is a decrease of about 40%; the "60%" is
  the ratio. The other percentages (k01 -50%, k02 -90%, Dur1 +90%, Dur2
  +1300%, AUC -23%) agree with Table 1 as decreases or increases.
* **Dose.** Doses are of lidocaine hydrochloride and concentrations are of
  lidocaine, as in the paper; CL/F and V/F absorb the salt factor and the
  unknown bioavailability.
* **Covariates.** CL/F and V/F are per kg (Table 1 units); no other covariates
  were tested. The isoflurane anaesthesia during the block and the
  medetomidine/butorphanol premedication may have influenced disposition, as
  the authors discuss.
